opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's an empirical question, and my intuitions have shifted a lot over the years. When we started on AlphaFold, there was a strong temptation to build in everything we knew about proteins: the physics, the geometry, the chemistry. Some of that turned out to matter, but often not in the way we expected. The things that helped most weren't hard-coded answers. They were ways of structuring the problem so the network could learn the right thing more easily.

So I'd frame it less as "program the concept in" versus "let it learn," and more as: what inductive biases make the learning problem tractable given the data you have? If you have a near-infinite amount of data, like with text, next-token prediction can discover remarkable structure on its own. Our hand-designed concepts are often worse than what the model finds, because we're imposing a human abstraction that may be convenient for us but isn't actually the most useful representation.

But in science you're often in a data-limited regime. The Protein Data Bank is precious, but it's not the internet. There, a well-chosen bias, like respecting the geometry of three-dimensional space or letting the model reason iteratively about pairs of residues, can be worth orders of magnitude of data. The key is to build in the constraints you're very confident are true, like symmetries, and to be humble about the ones that are just your current theory of how things work.

The failure mode I've seen many times is a researcher putting their favorite concept into the architecture, then spending a year discovering the model would have done better without it. So my rule of thumb is to build in structure, not conclusions. Give the model the right space to think in, and let the data tell it what to think.

r001.rationale: The response says next-token prediction can discover structure on its own and contrasts that with hard-coding conclusions, communicating that learning can produce useful structure without explicit programming.

r002.rationale: It challenges hard-coding a researcher’s preferred concept, saying hand-designed concepts can be worse than what the model finds and advising that we build in structure rather than conclusions.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes the setting with near-infinite data, where next-token prediction can discover remarkable structure, from data-limited settings where useful learning depends on appropriate inductive biases.

r004.rationale: It frames the issue as empirical and asks what biases make learning tractable with available data, noting that a well-chosen bias can be worth orders of magnitude of data.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this is one of those questions where my instinct has shifted over the years, and AlphaFold is actually a good case study in why.

When we started on AlphaFold 2, there was a very live question of how much physics and chemistry to bake into the architecture. We knew a lot about proteins. We know bond lengths, we know angles, we know a great deal about how amino acids interact. And the temptation is to write all of that down as hard constraints and let the network fill in the rest. What we found, repeatedly, was that the places where we put in strong explicit structure were often the places where the model underperformed, and the places where we gave it a softer inductive bias, something like "here is a representation that makes it easy to reason about pairs of residues" or "here is an operation that respects rotations and translations," were the places where it took off. The structure module reasons about rigid bodies, and that matters, but it learned the chemistry rather than having it hardcoded. We didn't tell it what a hydrogen bond was. It figured that out because it needed to.

So my general view is that the right thing to program in is not the concept but the shape of the space the concept lives in. You want to give the model the right coordinate system, the right symmetries, the right way to pass information around, and then let the actual content be learned from data. Explicit concepts tend to be our approximation of the truth, and the model can usually find a better one if you don't get in its way. The failure mode of hand-programming representations is that you lock in your own misunderstandings.

Now, on the next-token prediction side, I think the interesting thing is that it's a remarkably good objective precisely because it's so unopinionated. It doesn't tell the model what concepts to have. It just says, predict the world, and whatever internal structure helps you do that, build it. And the evidence from language models is that this produces representations that look conceptual, that generalize, that compose. Nobody wrote down "syntax" or "arithmetic" and yet something like those emerges.

Where I'd push back on the pure "just scale it and let it learn" position is that data efficiency really matters, and inductive bias is how you buy data efficiency. In biology we don't have the internet's worth of protein structures. We had something like a hundred and seventy thousand structures in the PDB, which is tiny by language model standards. There was no way a generic architecture was going to learn the geometry of proteins from that. We had to be opinionated about the architecture to make the data go far enough. So I don't think it's one or the other. It's a question of how much data you have, how much you actually know with confidence, and whether the thing you know is a constraint on the answer or just a constraint on the search space. The second kind is almost always the better thing to program in.

And honestly, I'd say the biggest lesson for me is to be humble about what you think the model needs. Every time we tried to be clever about explicitly encoding a concept, there was a version where the network could learn it better, provided we'd given it the right tools to represent it. The art is in designing those tools, not in writing the answer down.

r001.rationale: The response says next-token prediction can produce conceptual representations, with syntax and arithmetic emerging without being explicitly specified.

r002.rationale: It argues that models need not have concepts hardcoded: provide useful structure and tools, then let the model learn the concepts.

r003.rationale: It describes next-token prediction as a good objective and says conceptual representations emerge, but does not distinguish merely doing the task from doing it well enough to develop conceptual understanding.

r004.rationale: It discusses data efficiency and using inductive bias, but does not identify acquiring learned conceptual representations at lower computational or data cost as an unresolved question.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a bit of a false dichotomy there. You always put something into the model: an architecture, a training objective, a choice of data. The question is which parts of the problem you want to specify, and which parts you want the model to discover.

With AlphaFold, we put in quite a lot of structure associated with the problem. We know we’re trying to predict something in three-dimensional space, and we know that rotating a protein doesn’t change what it is. Those are useful things to build in. But we don’t want to write down a complete theory of how every interaction determines the structure. Learning that is a large part of the point.

Next-token prediction is interesting because a relatively simple objective can demand very sophisticated internal representations. To predict what comes next, it may help to understand what’s happening. But I’d distinguish between saying that the objective can produce useful concepts and saying that it necessarily produces all the concepts we want, in a form we can reliably use.

So I’d approach this experimentally. Does putting a particular structure into the model help it learn more efficiently? Does it generalize better? Or have we imposed a constraint that gets in the way? I don’t think we should be committed to either putting everything in or learning everything from scratch.

r001.rationale: It says a simple next-token objective can lead to sophisticated internal representations and useful concepts, while distinguishing learned structure from what is built in.

r002.rationale: Calling the choice a false dichotomy and noting that the model can learn concepts challenges the idea that all useful concepts need to be explicitly built into it.

r003.rationale: The response says next-token prediction may benefit from understanding, but does not distinguish mere prediction from prediction performed well enough to develop conceptual understanding.

r004.rationale: It frames as an open experimental question whether adding structure helps the model learn more efficiently, which addresses acquiring learned structure at lower cost.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a bit of a false dichotomy, because you’re always putting something into the model. You choose the architecture, the data, the objective, and what information it gets to see. So the question is really: what do you want to build in, and what do you want to leave for learning?

With AlphaFold, we built in quite a lot of structure about the problem. We knew that geometry mattered. But that’s different from specifying exactly how the model should recognize a particular interaction or assemble a protein. You want to provide a useful language for solving the problem without writing the solution yourself.

The risk with explicitly programming conceptual representations is that your concepts may be incomplete. You can make it very easy for the model to express what you already understand and very difficult for it to express something you haven’t thought of. Learning representations gives you a chance to get beyond that.

At the same time, I wouldn’t assume that next-token prediction will produce every representation you might need, simply because it can learn very rich ones. What matters is whether the training signal actually rewards the distinctions that matter for your problem. I’d approach that experimentally: does adding a particular structure make the system learn better, generalize better, or use less data? That seems more useful than having a philosophical commitment to either building everything in or learning everything from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response says learning representations can help the model go beyond what was explicitly specified, but does not state that predicting data well induces useful intermediate representations.

r002.rationale: It argues that explicitly programmed concepts may be incomplete and distinguishes giving a model a useful problem-solving language from specifying the solution itself.

r003.rationale: It says rich representations do not follow from next-token prediction alone; the training signal must reward the distinctions relevant to the problem.

r004.rationale: It suggests checking whether added structure reduces data use, but does not identify acquiring learned conceptual representations at lower computational or data cost as an unresolved question.
